query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?
task_summary: Inferring Powder Cohesion And Friction From Auger Doser Discharge Data Validated Against Standard Flow Tests

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.

    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. Abstract:
<jats:p><p>The flow of abrasive particles in the pressurized feed system of an abrasive jet micro machining (AJM) apparatus was investigated both experimentally and computationally. The feasibility of predicting the abrasive mass flow rate using discrete element methods implemented in two commercial software packages, i.e. LS-DYNA and EDEM, was studied. A method to simulate applied pressure was developed, and computer codes to extract relative data during postprocessing were implemented. For a simplified system using spherical particles, the EDEM results better agreed with measured mass flow rates, while LS-DYNA software grossly underestimated the measured mass flow rate. The effect of pressure on mass flow rate was studied numerically using EDEM and the trends largely agreed with the experiments. Overall, it is possible to use discrete element methods to simulate powder flow in AJM systems, but only at an exceptionally high computational cost, and with considerable effort to extract relevant data.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
Powder processing and manufacturing operations are rate processes for which the bottleneck is cohesive powder flow. Diversity of material properties, particulate form, and sensitivity to environmental conditions, such as humidity and tribo-electric charging, make its prediction very challenging. However, this is highly desirable particularly when addressing a powder material for which only a small quantity is available. Furthermore, in a number of applications powder flow testing at low stress levels is highly desirable. Characterisation of bulk powder failure for flow initiation (quasi-static) is well established. However, bulk flow parameters are all sensitive to strain rate with which the powder is sheared, but in contrast to quasi-static test methods, there is no shear cell for characterisation of the bulk parameters in the dynamic regime. There are only a handful of instruments available for powder rheometry, in which the bulk resistance to motion can be quantified as a function of the shear strain rate, but the challenge is relating the bulk behaviour to the physical and mechanical properties of constituting particles. A critique of the current state of the art in characterisation and analysis of cohesive powder flow is presented, addressing the effects of cohesion, strain rate, fluid medium drag and particle shape.

Abstract:
<jats:p>To achieve precise feeding, this study coupled a Discrete Element Method (DEM)-based virtual test platform with the Response Surface Method (RSM) to quantitatively evaluate and optimize the effects of traveling speed (X₁), scraper rotation speed (X₂), and conveyor belt speed (X₃) on unit feeding amount (Y₁) and feeding uniformity (Y₂). A simplified core model of the feeding device was established in EDEM, and the cohesive characteristics of Total Mixed Ration (TMR) were characterized using the Hertz–Mindlin with JKR Cohesion contact model. A three-factor, three-level Box–Behnken experimental design was employed to fit quadratic regression models for Y₁ and Y₂. The results indicated that both models were statistically significant (P < 0.0001). The significant influencing factors for Y₁ were ranked as X₁ > X₂ > X₃, while those for Y₂ were ranked as X₂ > X₃ > X₁. Based on the analysis of interaction effects among parameters and multi-objective desirability optimization (targeting Y₁ = 10–12 kg·m⁻¹ and maximizing Y₂), the optimal combination was determined as X₁ = 3.05 km·h⁻¹, X₂ = 84.9 r·min⁻¹, and X₃ = 326.5 r·min⁻¹. After rounding for engineering application, X₁ = 3 km·h⁻¹, X₂ = 85 r·min⁻¹, and X₃ = 330 r·min⁻¹ yielded verification results of Y₁ = 11.49 kg·m⁻¹ and Y₂ = 91.54%, with prediction deviations below 5%. Within the studied geometric and parameter ranges, the material flow remained continuous and stable, without persistent arching or blockage. Therefore, the analysis primarily focused on uniformity and throughput. This study provides executable operational parameters and a transferable parameter design approach applicable to cohesive feed systems</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing (AM) has been adopted by various industries as a novel manufacturing technology. Powder spreading is a crucial part of the LPBF AM process that defines the quality of the fabricated objects. In this study, the impacts of various input parameters on the spread of powder density and particle distribution during the powder spreading process are investigated using the DEM (discrete element method) simulation tool. The DEM simulations extend over several powder layers and are used to analyze the powder particle packing density variation in different layers and at different points along the longitudinal spreading direction. Additionally, this research covers experimental measurements of the density of the powder packing and the powder particle size distribution on the construction plate.

Abstract:
Producing dense and homogeneous powder layers with smooth free surface is challenging in additive manufacturing, as interparticle cohesion can strongly affect the powder packing structure and therefore influence the quality of the end product. We use the Discrete Element Method to simulate the spreading process of spherical powders and examine how cohesion influences the characteristics of the packing structure with a focus on the fluctuation of the local morphology. As cohesion increases, the overall packing density decreases, and the free surface roughness increases, which is calculated from digitized surface height distributions. Local structural fluctuations for both quantities are examined through the local packing anisotropy on the particle scale, obtained from Voronoï tessellation. The distributions of these particle-level metrics quantify the increasingly heterogeneous packing structure with clustering and changing surface morphology.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder bed fusion (PBF) is a widely adopted additive manufacturing (AM) process category that enables high-resolution fabrication across metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites. However, its inherent process complexity demands robust modeling to ensure quality, reliability, and scalability. This review provides a critical synthesis of advances in physics-based simulations, machine learning, and digital twin frameworks for PBF. We analyze progress across scales—from micro-scale melt pool dynamics and mesoscale track stability to part-scale residual stress predictions—while highlighting the growing role of hybrid physics–data-driven approaches in capturing process–structure–property (PSP) relationships. Special emphasis is given to the integration of real-time sensing, multi-scale modeling, and AI-enhanced optimization, which together form the foundation of emerging PBF digital twins. Key challenges—including computational cost, data scarcity, and model interoperability—are critically examined, alongside opportunities for scalable, interpretable, and industry-ready digital twin platforms. By outlining both the current state-of-the-art and future research priorities, this review positions digital twins as a transformative paradigm for advancing PBF toward reliable, high-quality, and industrially scalable manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Understanding biofilm rheology is crucial for industrial and domestic food safety practices. This comprehensive review addresses the knowledge gap on the rheology of biofilm. Specifically, the review explores the influence of fluid flow, shear stress, and substrate properties on the initiation, structure, and functionality of biofilms, as essential implications for food safety. The viscosity and shear-thinning characteristics of non-Newtonian fluids may impact the attachment and detachment dynamics of biofilms, influencing their stability and resilience under different flow conditions. The discussion spans multiple facets, including the role of extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs) in biofilm formation, the impact of rheological attributes of biofilm on their adhesion to surfaces, and the influence of shear forces between biofilms and substrate's surface characteristics on biofilm stability. Analytical techniques, encompassing rheometry, microscopy, and molecular biology approaches, are scrutinized for their contributions to understanding these interactions. The paper delves into the implications for the food industry, highlighting potential risks associated with biofilm formation and proposing strategies for effective control and prevention. Future research directions and the integration of rheological considerations into food safety regulations are underscored as pivotal steps in mitigating biofilm-related risks. The synthesis of microbiology, materials science, and engineering perspectives offers a multidimensional exploration of rheology–biofilm interactions, laying the groundwork for informed interventions in diverse industrial settings.

Abstract:
The pharmaceutical industry is undergoing a paradigm shift towards continuous processing from batch, where continuous direct compression (CDC) is considered to offer the most straightforward implementation amongst powder processes due to the relatively low number of unit operations or handling steps. Due to the nature of continuous processing, the bulk properties of the formulation will require sufficient flowability and tabletability in order to be processed and transported effectively to and from each unit operation. Powder cohesion presents one of the greatest obstacles to the CDC process as it inhibits powder flow. As a result, there have been many studies investigating potential manners in which to overcome the effects of cohesion with, to date, little consideration of how these controls may affect downstream unit operations. The aim of this literature review is to explore and consolidate this literature, considering the impact of powder cohesion and cohesion control measures on the three-unit operations of the CDC process (feeding, mixing, and tabletting). This review will also cover the consequences of implementing such control measures whilst highlighting subject matter which could be of value for future research to better understand how to manage cohesive powders for CDC manufacture.

The excerpt identifies Lopez et al. [55] as an original DEM study examining how interparticle cohesion affects powder feeding in a conveying screw/auger system. The stated methodology was to assign particle physical properties and shape for paracetamol, then conduct a forward sensitivity analysis by varying adhesive stiffness (Kadh) and conveying impeller rotation rate. At fixed rotation speed, increasing Kadh increased particle translational velocity in the conveying barrel, while changing conveying speed had a stronger effect on hopper velocity than changing cohesion over the tested range. The study also evaluated average mass discharged per watt and found an exponential decline as Kadh increased; Kadh values above 0.5 produced arching/bridging and inconsistent screw filling, causing irregular mass flow. However, this excerpt does not describe inverse calibration of cohesion or friction from measured feeder mass-flow/feed-variability data. It also does not report independent validation of DEM parameters against ring-shear or other shear-cell tests. Thus, based on the excerpt, Lopez et al. represents DEM forward parameter sensitivity and mechanistic feeding analysis, not demonstrated inverse identification or independently shear-cell-validated calibration. The passage gives only citation [55], not the study’s full bibliographic details.

Abstract:
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropriate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM parameters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied. Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Abstract:
Powder bed-based additive manufacturing processes offer an extended freedom in design and enable the processing of metals, ceramics, and polymers with a high level of relative density. The latter is a prevalent measure of process and component quality, which depends on various input variables. A key point in this context is the condition of powder beds. To enhance comprehension of their particle-level formation and facilitate process optimization, simulations based on the Discrete Element Method are increasingly employed in research. To generate qualitatively as well as quantitatively reliable simulation results, an adaptation of the contact model parameterization is necessary. However, current adaptation methods often require the implementation of models that significantly increase computational effort, therefore limiting their applicability. To counteract this obstacle, a sophisticated formula-based adaptation and evaluation method is presented in this research. Additionally, the developed method enables accelerated parameter determination with limited experimental effort. Thus, it represents an integrative component, which supports further research efforts based on the Discrete Element Method by significantly reducing the parameterization effort. The universal nature of deducting this method also allows its adaptation to similar parameterization problems and its implementation in other fields of research.

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The search for efficient, durable, and scalable catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is hampered by the slow innovation cycles for advanced materials. Here, we present
                    <jats:italic>FastCat</jats:italic>
                    —an artificial intelligence (AI)‐orchestrated self‐driving closed‐loop materials discovery system for the autonomous discovery of platinum group metal free multimetal hydroxides for alkaline water electrolysis. With FastCat, we have synthesized, characterized, and tested more than 500 Ni‐based multielement layered double hydroxide OER catalysts. In one of the largest AI‐orchestrated catalyst discovery campaigns to date, our metaheuristic Bayesian optimization identified known high‐performance compositions and several novel multielement Ni–Fe–Cr–Co alloys with unprecedented overpotentials as low as 231 mV at 20 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    and compositional ratios approaching  at higher current densities. FastCat can synthesize and electrochemically test up to 75 material compositions daily without human interaction. It can optimize the composition by analyzing trends in the test results, validating their reproducibility, and testing durability. This study includes measurements of >1000 samples, making it one of the largest autonomous experimental electrocatalysis datasets to date, and the findings showcase how autonomous materials discovery can make complex, multielement compositions accessible for research and drastically accelerate the development of novel materials.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
One dominant challenge facing the development of biorefineries is achieving consistent system throughput with highly variant biomass feedstock quality and handling performance. Current handling unit operations are adapted from other sectors (primarily agriculture), where some simplifying assumptions about granular mechanics and flow performance do not translate well to a highly compressible and anisotropic material with nonlinear time- and stress-dependent properties. This work explores the shear and frictional properties of loblolly pine at multiple experimental test apparatus and particle scales to elucidate a property window that defines the shear behavior over a range of material attributes (particle size, size distribution, moisture content, etc.). In general, it was observed that the bulk internal friction and apparent cohesion depend strongly on both the stress state of the sample in granular shear testers and the overall particle size and distribution span. For equipment designed to characterize the quasi-static shear stress failure of bulk materials ranging from 50 to 1,000 ml in test volume, similar test results were observed for finely milled particles (50% passing size of 1.4 mm) with a narrow size distribution (span between 10 and 90% passing size of 0.9 mm), while stress chaining and over-torque issues persisted for the bench-scale test apparatus for larger particle sizes or widely dispersed sample sizes. Measurement of the anisotropic particle–particle friction ranged from coefficients of approximately 0.20 to 0.45 and resulted in significantly higher and more variable friction measurements for larger particle sizes and in perpendicular alignment orientations. To supplement these laboratory-scale properties, this work explores the flow of loblolly pine and Douglas fir through a pilot-scale wedge-shaped hopper and a screw feeder. For the gravity-driven hopper flow, the critical arching distance and mass discharge rate ranged from approximately 10 to 30 mm and 2 to 16 tons/hour, respectively, for both materials, where the arching distance depends strongly on the overall particle size and depends less on the hopper inclination angle. Comparatively, the auger feeder was found to be much more impacted by the size of the particles, where smaller particles had a more consistent and stable flow while consuming less power.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Relevance of the work. The Hopper and Bin design is the most commonly used technique of storing materials as it is a gravity fed system and is generally used for storing materials such as agricultural grains as well as mined minerals such as sand and coal. Mass flow, which is ideally the most desired flow type sees the bulk material travel uniformly with all particles in motion until all the material leaves the bin. The other types of flow generally occur with flat-bottomed bins with shallow hoppers are not seen as ideal as with this design problems such as arching and rat holing occur. The issue with the current design is that some of the material becomes stagnant in the bin, this can be costly as if the bulk material becomes stuck, degradation can occur over time. It can be observed for the Funnel and Expanded flow, the rat holing and arching occurring due to the stagnant material. Research Objective is to design a novel mass flow acrylic bin and hopper to store bulk quantities of sand without stagnation or degradation Methodology. Two separate experimental procedures were carried out including the measurement of the specific gravity of the sand, shear test and final hopper design. The data was then manipulated and plotted stress transformations and identified multiple key flow property constituents. Using values such as the yield loci and associative yield stresses the hopper half angle α and opening diameter B were tabulated. Results and Conclusions. The optimum opening diameter B for an uncompacted system is 2 mm and the hopper half angle α adjusted to 34.58o , this was tested and provided a successful mass flow hopper system. Overall, the techniques used with specific gravity and shear cell testing gave a sufficient insight into the appropriate procedure for designing efficient and accurate bin and hoppers. Then substituting the values gathered into the appropriate formulae provided a successful mass flow system for the intended bulk material which is sand.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser-based powder bed fusion (LPBF) of metals offers the unique possibility of creating the microstructure voxel-by-voxel. The minimum voxel size in each direction is dependent on material dosing accuracy coupled with laser processing parameters. The rapid solidification conditions during LPBF lead to material heterogeneity coupled with hierarchical and non-equilibrium microstructures. The current paper delves into two different pathways available currently to control microstructure in LPBF, namely: in-situ microstructure control through material distribution to form functionally graded components with complex interfaces; application of post-processing thermo-mechanical treatments to control the microstructure. Unlike traditional manufacturing methods, each voxel in LPBF can be further processed multiple times after the first fusion process. Such in-situ processing presents further opportunity for tailoring the microstructure of each voxel in 3D. A future perspective is thus offered on the opportunities to control and engineer LPBF microstructures in metals.

A multivariate regression parametric study on DEM input parameters
of free‑flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data‑based
validation

Bilal El‑Kassem1,2 · Nizar Salloum2 · Thomas Brinz2 · Yousef Heider1     · Bernd Markert1


Received: 25 September 2019 / Revised: 10 December 2019 / Accepted: 10 January 2020 / Published online: 29 January 2020
© The Author(s) 2020

Abstract
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropri-
ate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an
alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM param-
eters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied.
Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model
and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six
DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size,
Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass
flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive
powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and
the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in
both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Keywords  Discrete element method · Free-flowing powder · Cohesive powder · Design of experiment · Multivariate
regression analysis · Angle of repose

From text 'jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 43-44'.

Owen Jones-Salkey, Zoe Chu, Andrew Ingram, and Christopher R. K. Windows-Yule. Reviewing the impact of powder cohesion on continuous direct compression (cdc) performance. Pharmaceutics, 15:1587, May 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics15061587, doi:10.3390/pharmaceutics15061587. This article has 39 citations.

The cited studies most directly relevant to powder properties, feeder precision, variability, screw rate, and hopper-fill effects include Engisch and Muzzio (2012), which concerns characterization of loss-in-weight feeders, and Engisch and Muzzio (2015), which specifically examines feedrate deviations caused by hopper refill. Kehlenbeck and Sommer (2003) addresses short-term dosing constancy in volumetric feeders. Bekaert et al. (2022) studies long-term material processability during continuous feeding, while Yadav et al. (2019) links material properties and equipment configuration to loss-in-weight feeder performance. Shier et al. (2022) develops a predictive gravimetric-feeding model based on an API-rich materials-property library. López et al. (2020) is the most explicitly screw/auger-focused DEM study, analyzing screw feeding of faceted particles; however, the excerpt does not indicate that it links shear-cell flow function to dose precision or variability. Related references cover powder flow characterization (Krantz et al., 2009), rotating-drum flow measurement (Neveu et al., 2022), and process-induced tribocharging during twin-screw feeding (Beretta et al., 2020). The excerpt separately cites Windows-Yule and Neveu (2022) on DEM calibration, but provides no evidence of a study that simultaneously inverts DEM parameters from feeder response and independently validates them against shear testing. That specific combined methodology cannot be confirmed from this reference list.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6'.

Owen Jones-Salkey, Zoe Chu, Andrew Ingram, and Christopher R. K. Windows-Yule. Reviewing the impact of powder cohesion on continuous direct compression (cdc) performance. Pharmaceutics, 15:1587, May 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics15061587, doi:10.3390/pharmaceutics15061587. This article has 39 citations.

The excerpt identifies Lopez et al. [55] as a DEM study directly examining how powder cohesion, represented by adhesive stiffness (Kadh), affects screw-feeder behavior. At a fixed conveying-impeller speed, increasing Kadh increased particle translational velocity in the conveying barrel, with a smaller effect at the barrel–hopper interface. Conversely, at fixed Kadh, increasing conveying speed increased particle velocity, and conveying speed had a greater influence on hopper particle velocity than cohesion over the tested range. The study also assessed power efficiency: average mass discharged per watt decreased exponentially as Kadh increased. Above Kadh = 0.5, cohesive forces produced arching or bridging, which caused inconsistent screw filling and therefore irregular mass flow. The excerpt does not report dose precision, dose variability, or hopper-fill measurements as independently validated outcomes, nor does it describe a study that simultaneously inverted DEM parameters from feed-response data and independently validated those parameters using shear-cell testing. The surrounding discussion does link shear-cell-derived flow function/cohesion measurements to powder flow generally, and reports that colloidal silica can alter cohesion and FFC, but it does not connect those measurements directly to screw-dose precision in the cited material.

From text 'bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8'.

Davide Bascone, Federico Galvanin, Nilay Shah, and Salvador Garcia-Munoz. Hybrid mechanistic-empirical approach to the modeling of twin screw feeders for continuous tablet manufacturing. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 59:6650-6661, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00420. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt identifies several studies and approaches linking powder properties and operating variables to screw-feeder performance. It states that cohesion, particle descriptors, compressibility, rheology, flow, permeability, and porosity can significantly affect feeding. It also cites Engish and Muzzio’s statistical characterization of loss-in-weight feeders, which used relative standard deviation and ANOVA to evaluate the effects of feeder tooling, powder, and screw speed on feeder performance. Other cited work used data-driven response-surface or kriging models, multivariate methods, and semi-empirical models involving hopper powder pressure and feed factor. Physics-based models relate feed rate to volumetric efficiency, screw fullness, bulk density, screw speed, and screw geometry. The featured hybrid model estimates hopper stress, converts it to effective powder density through an empirical relationship, incorporates screw geometry and vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and predicts dynamic mass flow. DEM is described as useful for predicting packing, mass flow, and mixing, but requiring substantial computation and calibration of particle properties. The excerpt does not mention shear-cell flow-function testing, dose precision specifically, or a study that simultaneously inverts DEM parameters from feed-response data and independently validates them against shear testing.

Yifan Wang. Using multivariate analysis for pharmaceutical drug product development. ArXiv, Jan 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.7282/t39z9770, doi:10.7282/t39z9770. This article has 10 citations.

The excerpt identifies several lines of work relevant to powder screw-feeder and auger dosing. It states that feeder performance depends on equipment design, control system, target flow rate, and powder flow properties, with poor powder–feeder matching producing sticking and high feed-rate variability. It specifically reports that Freeman et al. correlated two dynamic powder properties with the volumetric flow rate of different screw feeders. It also notes work on feeder steady-state characterization, performance during hopper refill, refill scheduling, discharge proportioning, and vibratory hopper agitation to improve flow and feeding precision. Owen et al. applied the Discrete Element Method to predict screw-conveyor performance as a function of operating conditions, but the excerpt explicitly says that material properties were not included in that model. The passage emphasizes that powder flowability is multidimensional and that a single characterization technique is insufficient for predicting feeder performance. The described study therefore uses multiple measurements—including shear-cell-derived angle of internal friction, dimensionless cohesion, compressibility, permeability, and dynamic flow properties—alongside volumetric and gravimetric feeder tests. PCA is used for similarity comparisons, while PLSR predicts feeder performance and optimal tooling from material-property inputs. No evidence in this excerpt indicates a study that simultaneously inverts DEM parameters from feed-response data and independently validates those parameters against shear testing.

The excerpt identifies Bascone et al. (2020) as a study of twin-screw feeders for continuous tablet manufacturing using a hybrid mechanistic-empirical first-order-plus-dead-time model. It investigates different powders and two screw geometries, relating feeder response to operating conditions including screw speed and to bulk-solid properties. The feeder is described as a hopper, flow-aid system, and one or two conveying screws; mass flow is controlled by weighing the feeder and adjusting screw speed, while refill periods operate in volumetric/open-loop mode. The introduction emphasizes that feed-rate accuracy is essential and that cohesive or poorly flowing powders are difficult to meter. It lists cohesion, particulate descriptors, and compressibility among properties that can affect feeder performance, but the supplied pages do not provide specific dose-precision or variability correlations, nor do they describe a shear-cell flow-function analysis. The excerpt also does not report DEM parameter inversion from feed-response data or independent validation against shear testing. It instead frames the work as addressing limited first-principles understanding through a hybrid model and reports good predictions for 35-mm screws, with restricted validity for the least cohesive powders using 20-mm screws.

The corresponding pilot-scale tests found that hopper critical arching distance and mass discharge rate depend strongly on overall particle size, while auger-feeder behavior is even more sensitive to particle size: smaller particles produced more consistent and stable flow and consumed less power. These findings are relevant to linking powder or biomass properties with feeder flow stability, but the excerpt does not mention dose precision, dosing variability, screw rate, or hopper-fill level as measured response variables. Abstract:
The gut microbiota has emerged as a key human health and disease determinant. However, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the composition, diversity, and function of the gut microbiota, specifically in the African population. This scoping review aims to examine the existing literature on gut microbiota research conducted in Africa, providing an overview of the current knowledge and identifying research gaps. A comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant studies. Databases including MEDLINE (PubMed), African Index Medicus (AIM), CINAHL (EBSCOhost), Science Citation index (Web of Science), Embase (Ovid), Scopus (Elsevier), WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and Google Scholar were searched for relevant articles. Studies investigating the gut microbiota in African populations of all age groups were included. The initial screening included a total of 2136 articles, of which 154 were included in this scoping review. The current scoping review revealed a limited number of studies investigating diseases of public health significance in relation to the gut microbiota. Among these studies, HIV (14.3%), colorectal cancer (5.2%), and diabetes mellitus (3.9%) received the most attention. The top five countries that contributed to gut microbiota research were South Africa (16.2%), Malawi (10.4%), Egypt (9.7%), Kenya (7.1%), and Nigeria (6.5%). The high number (n = 66) of studies that did not study any specific disease in relation to the gut microbiota remains a gap that needs to be filled. This scoping review brings attention to the prevalent utilization of observational study types (38.3%) in the studies analysed and emphasizes the importance of conducting more experimental studies. Furthermore, the findings reflect the need for more disease-focused, comprehensive, and population-specific gut microbiota studies across diverse African regions and ethnic groups to better understand the factors shaping gut microbiota composition and its implications for health and disease. Such knowledge has the potential to inform targeted interventions and personalized approaches for improving health outcomes in African populations.

Abstract:
As an emerging new class, metal nanoparticles and especially silver nanoparticles hold great potential in the field of cancer biology. Due to cancer-specific targeting, the consequently attenuated side-effects and the massive anti-cancer features render nanoparticle therapeutics desirable platforms for clinically relevant drug development. In this review, we highlight those characteristics of silver nanoparticle-based therapeutic concepts that are unique, exploitable, and achievable, as well as those that represent the critical hurdle in their advancement to clinical utilization. Abstract:
Cross-stream cutters are widely used in the mining and resources industry to obtain representative samples of particulate flows. Discrete element modelling (DEM) and analysis can be used to investigate influences of operational parameters, sampler design and material physical properties in the generation of the Increment Extraction Error (IEE), which when present, results in a frequently biased, non-representative sample. The study investigates the practicality of the rules and recommendations proposed by Dr. Pierre Gy that were developed and established as principles for the correct extraction of samples in industrial sampling equipment. Results validate Pierre Gy’s sampling theory using DEM in a cross-stream cutter of a sulphide gold plant. Importantly, the outcomes indicate that careful consideration must be given to physical ore properties and, consequently, that sampling systems should be developed specifically to each application.

Abstract:
<jats:p>High-fidelity models (HFMs) for twin-screw wet granulation (TSWG) are often too computationally expensiv//e for routine calibration, optimization, and digital twin deployment. This chapter presents a faster, cheaper, and easier-to-use surrogate modeling workflow that preserves HFM-level predictive capability. Sensitivity analysis is applied to prioritize influential inputs, and a rate mechanism global system analysis reduces the calibration space by 60%, leaving only 10 critical parameters. Using this reduced set, a compact mechanistic surrogate comprising 10 equations achieves accurate particle size distribution (PSD) predictions with an R of 0.998 and a simulation time of 0.41 seconds. In addition, a hybrid TSWG model is developed by coupling a population balance model (PBM) with an artificial neural network (ANN). The ANN provides rapid first-pass estimates of kinetic rate parameters within the calibration range, which are then integrated into the PBM to refine PSD predictions and accelerate calibration. The proposed workflow, adaptive framework for robust and accelerated model evaluation (AFRAME), offers a structured and efficient methodology for model calibration in continuous pharmaceutical manufacturing and supports the development of robust, adaptive digital twins applicable to a broader range of manufacturing processes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Content uniformity (CU) of the active pharmaceutical ingredient is a critical quality attribute of tablets as a dosage form, ensuring reproducible drug potency. Failure to meet the accepted uniformity in the final product may be caused either by suboptimal mixing and insufficient initial blend homogeneity, or may result from further particle segregation during storage, transfer or the compression process itself. This review presents the most relevant powder segregation mechanisms in tablet manufacturing and summarizes the currently available, up-to-date research on segregation and uniformity loss at the various stages of production process—the blend transfer from the bulk container to the tablet press, filling and discharge from the feeding hopper, as well as die filling. Formulation and processing factors affecting the occurrence of segregation and tablets’ CU are reviewed and recommendations for minimizing the risk of content uniformity failure in tablets are considered herein, including the perspective of continuous manufacturing.

Abstract:
Vibratory screens are used in mining to classify mineral and send it to different pathways, normally using conveyor belts. Vibration analysis techniques are commonly used for condition monitoring and early detection of unforeseen failures to generate predictive maintenance. This paper proposes a novel solution to implement wireless sensors forming an instrumentation dedicated network combined with data-driven machine learning for monitoring vibrating screens. The system is optimized explicitly for vibratory equipment, which sets it apart from general-purpose condition monitoring systems. Embedded sensors are battery-powered and robust to withstand constant vibratory movement. The data used for training the machine learning models are gathered from a lab setup and discrete element simulations. The test bench consisted of a lab-scale vibratory screener, in which 3-axis accelerations, cumulative damage and wear are measured using sensors embedded in the rubber screens. Proposed data-driven machine learning models classify each screen condition in states according to the ISO 2372 standards for vibration severity. The system can identify random failures (based on test bench measured data) as progressive degradation failures over time (based on discrete element methods simulation results). The accuracy of the classification algorithms consistently ranges from 95% to 98%. Moreover, the system allows the early detection of unacceptable states up to 168 hours before the screen’s end-of-life predation by an expert. The system is characterized for (i) avoiding unplanned downtime and consequently (ii) increase operational availability. The system is intended to notify users when an abnormal operation is detected and impending failure events in the early stage.

Abstract:
The continuous twin-screw wet granulation (TSWG) process was investigated and optimized with prediction-oriented I-optimal designs. The I-optimal designs can not only obtain a precise estimation of the parameters that describe the effect of five input process parameters, including the screw speed, liquid-to-solid (L/S) ratio, TSWG feed rate, and numbers of the 30° and 60° mixing elements, on the granule quality in a TSWG process, but it can also provide a prediction of the response to determine the optimum operating conditions. Based on the constraints of the desired granule properties, a design space for the TSWG was determined, and the ranges of the operating parameters were defined. An acceptable degree of prediction was confirmed through validation experiments, demonstrating the reliability and effectiveness of using the I-optimal design method to study the TSWG process. The I-optimal design method can accelerate the screening and optimization of the TSWG process.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents an experimental workflow coupled with statistical tools to optimize L-DED processing parameters to build defect-free AlSi10Mg multilayer parts. Experimental steps included the quantitative evaluation of single beads, single layers, and multilayers to define L-DED processing windows. Regression and desirability functions, together with multi-objective Bayesian optimization, were used to optimize the main L-DED process parameters to meet target single-layer features. The systematic collection of reliable experimental data was critical to the success of the optimization models, and a detailed methodology is provided. The proposed workflow enabled the production of crack- and macroporosity-free multilayer parts with high geometrical accuracy and metallurgical bond integrity, achieving densities from 99.55% to 99.80% and deposition efficiencies between 87 and 97%, significantly exceeding previously reported values. This work provides practical guidelines to evaluate the outcomes of the AM L-DED process and obtain multilayer AlSi10Mg parts free from deleterious defects.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discerning assimilated diets of wild animals using stable isotopes is well established where potential dietary items in food webs are isotopically distinct. With the advent of mixing models, and Bayesian extensions of such models (Bayesian Stable Isotope Mixing Models, BSIMMs), statistical techniques available for these efforts have been rapidly increasing. The accuracy with which BSIMMs quantify diet, however, depends on several factors including uncertainty in tissue discrimination factors (TDFs; <jats:italic>Δ</jats:italic>) and identification of appropriate error structures. Whereas performance of BSIMMs has mostly been evaluated with simulations, here we test the efficacy of BSIMMs by raising domestic broiler chicks (<jats:italic>Gallus gallus domesticus</jats:italic>) on four isotopically distinct diets under controlled environmental conditions, ideal for evaluating factors that affect TDFs and testing how BSIMMs allocate individual birds to diets that vary in isotopic similarity. For both liver and feather tissues, <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic><jats:sup>13</jats:sup>C and <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic> <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>N values differed among dietary groups. <jats:italic>Δ</jats:italic><jats:sup>13</jats:sup>C of liver, but not feather, was negatively related to the rate at which individuals gained body mass. For <jats:italic>Δ</jats:italic><jats:sup>15</jats:sup>N, we identified effects of dietary group, sex, and tissue type, as well as an interaction between sex and tissue type, with females having higher liver <jats:italic>Δ</jats:italic><jats:sup>15</jats:sup>N relative to males. For both tissues, BSIMMs allocated most chicks to correct dietary groups, especially for models using combined TDFs rather than diet-specific TDFs, and those applying a multiplicative error structure. These findings provide new information on how biological processes affect TDFs and confirm that adequately accounting for variability in consumer isotopes is necessary to optimize performance of BSIMMs. Moreover, results demonstrate experimentally that these models reliably characterize consumed diets when appropriately parameterized.</jats:p>

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000018

From text 'bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 67-71'.

Pooja Rajendra Bhalode. Multi-scale modeling and analysis for pharmaceutical manufacturing. Text, Jan 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.7282/t3-jyg9-jd21, doi:10.7282/t3-jyg9-jd21. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes an inverse calibration procedure based on bulk measurements from a drawdown test, rather than clearly inverting DEM parameters from feeder discharge alone. Four DEM parameters were estimated from four measurements: angle of repose (30°), mass in the lower container (0.22 kg), shear angle (25°), and maximum flowrate (0.17 kg/s). The estimated parameters were particle static friction (PP_SF) = 0.4931, particle rolling friction (PP_RF) = 0.0383, particle coefficient of restitution (PP_COR) = 0.1851, and particle-wall static friction (PW_SF) = 0.195. The equations were solved by minimizing the sum of squared errors with GAMS/BARON, with an objective value of 4.2E-14. The dissertation also states that bulk measurements from the drawdown test depend on six DEM parameters, while four were estimated and other parameters were taken from the literature. The excerpt does not identify original DEM powder-spreading papers or provide paper-specific empirical comparisons validating spreading packing density, surface coverage, or roughness against measured powder properties. It does, however, describe the material factors relevant to transferring a feeder-calibrated DEM model to LPBF. Cohesion is especially important for LPBF powders below 100 μm: van der Waals, electrostatic, capillary, and chemical interactions promote agglomeration and reduce mobility. DEM models that omit cohesion overestimate powder mobility and fail to reproduce observed powder-bed characteristics, while cohesive energy density is often a highly influential calibration parameter. Particle morphology and surface texture also affect friction, contact stiffness, rearrangement, compaction, and flowability; spherical particles generally improve rearrangement and packing, whereas rough surfaces increase resistance to motion. PSD affects both packing and cohesion: broad distributions can improve packing through interstitial filling, but larger fractions of fine particles increase cohesive effects and may worsen flowability. The excerpt cautions that conventional feeder or flowability metrics are only indicators because LPBF spreading occurs in constrained geometries with layer thicknesses comparable to particle diameters. Therefore, transferring DEM calibration from feeder tests to LPBF requires process-specific validation and attention to cohesion, shape, PSD, and surface characteristics.

URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2020018, doi:10.14356/kona.2020018. This article has 90 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt documents several broad limitations of conventional cohesive-powder flow testing. Powder-flow prediction is highly sensitive to material properties, particle form, humidity, and tribo-electric charging, so environmental variability—including static-electric effects—complicates reproducible measurements. Quasi-static bulk-failure testing is described as well established, but the resulting bulk parameters depend on applied load and consolidation history and are sensitive to shear strain rate. Consequently, standard shear-cell methods do not adequately represent dynamic or high-rate flow: the authors state that no shear cell is available for characterising bulk parameters in the dynamic regime, while only a small number of powder rheometers quantify resistance to motion as a function of shear rate. Different commercial testers can also produce different quantitative values because cohesive powders form clusters whose size and packing depend on stress history and bulk structure. The excerpt emphasizes that low-stress testing is desirable in some applications, particularly where only small quantities of powder are available. For additive manufacturing, powder spreading is identified as critical, making flow and spreadability important concerns for processes such as LPBF. However, these pages do not specifically document Hall or Carney flow-test limitations, nor do they define or evaluate particular spreadability metrics for LPBF; those details would require later sections or another source.

The excerpt documents limitations of several dynamic powder-flow instruments, but it does not specifically discuss Hall or Carney flow tests, shear-cell testing at low versus high stresses, humidity effects, static electricity, or spreadability metrics for LPBF. For the Couette device, wall slip at the rotating inner cylinder can compromise measurements, the powder must be gripped at the walls to impose a no-slip condition, and the instrument requires a relatively large powder quantity. Its tall bed also experiences nonuniform gravity-induced stresses, anisotropic fabric, complex stress variations, and flow fields that may differ from the intended Couette shear. For the Anton Paar powder cell, results can vary with impeller geometry, and measurements taken at a fixed position may not represent the whole bed because of segregation, local aeration, and slipping. For the FT4 rheometer, Basic Flow Energy and Specific Energy are empirical dynamic measures based on impeller penetration and withdrawal. The article notes ongoing uncertainty about whether these energies reflect bulk friction or shear viscosity, and reports that a consistent direct correlation between measured flow energy and bulk mechanical or rheological properties has not been established. The excerpt only briefly connects powder flowability with additive manufacturing and provides no documented LPBF spreadability metric limitations.

For cohesive powders, dynamic tests are difficult to interpret because adhesive contacts produce clumps and adhesion is coupled with particle friction. Rotating-drum measurements can also promote segregation, reducing powder homogeneity and affecting the measured rheological response; cohesive beds additionally have irregular free surfaces, making flow parameters difficult to determine. The impact-based test also does not directly control penetration depth, so iterative adjustment of test conditions may be needed, while crater volume and impact velocity must be measured. In powder spreading, the excerpt identifies empty patches, size segregation, and transient jamming—particularly with narrow spreader gaps—as observable defects or process indicators.

From text 'faqih2006anexperimentalcomputationalapproach pages 8-9'.

AbdulMobeen Faqih, B. Chaudhuri, Albert W. Alexander, C. Davies, F. Muzzio, and M. Silvina Tomassone. An experimental/computational approach for examining unconfined cohesive powder flow. International journal of pharmaceutics, 324 2:116-27, Nov 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2006.05.067, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2006.05.067. This article has 85 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Faqih et al. (2006) directly couples an experimental gravity-discharge/flow signal with a discrete-element-method (DEM) model for unconfined cohesive powder flow. The computational objective is explicitly to relate inter-particle cohesive strength to GDR measurements. Cohesion is represented through a square-well potential producing a constant-intensity normal force during contact, parameterized by the Bond number K = Fcohes/mg. In the reported simulations, K was varied from 0 to 90: no avalanches occurred below K = 30, while discrete avalanches appeared for moderate and higher cohesion, particularly K > 45; values above 90 generated avalanches comparable to system size. Experimental flow behavior was quantified from the variance or standard deviation of the center-of-mass/weight signal versus vessel rotation rate. Increasing cohesion generally increased avalanche magnitude and the relative standard deviation, although overlapping avalanches at high speeds reduced the measured standard deviation. DEM validation used visual flow-region shape and local angle of repose, avalanche size, and material dilation. The excerpt does not provide details of a standard shear-cell validation protocol, nor does it discuss screw feeders. Therefore, it supports comparison with a screw feeder only at the general level: both systems can be studied through cohesion-dependent flow behavior, but the cited work concerns rotating-vessel gravity flow and avalanche/GDR metrics rather than continuous screw conveyance, torque, throughput, or feeder discharge.
