contexts.context: El‑Kassem et al. (2021) present a systematic DEM calibration framework using an optimized quadratic D‑optimal design and multivariate regression, not an auger doser. They varied six inputs—static/rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus, and cohesion energy density—and predicted five outputs: angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, and computation time. Experimental angle-of-repose tests validated the model for free-flowing and cohesive powders. Rolling friction strongly affected cohesive-powder repose angle, while static friction and particle size had minor roles; both friction coefficients strongly influenced porosity. The paper cites DEM screw-conveyor studies but does not demonstrate inverse feeder-based property inference or validation against shear-cell standards.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Lopez et al. [55] as a DEM study directly examining how powder cohesion, represented by adhesive stiffness (Kadh), affects screw-feeder behavior. At a fixed conveying-impeller speed, increasing Kadh increased particle translational velocity in the conveying barrel, with a smaller effect at the barrel–hopper interface. Conversely, at fixed Kadh, increasing conveying speed increased particle velocity, and conveying speed had a greater influence on hopper particle velocity than cohesion over the tested range. The study also assessed power efficiency: average mass discharged per watt decreased exponentially as Kadh increased. Above Kadh = 0.5, cohesive forces produced arching or bridging, which caused inconsistent screw filling and therefore irregular mass flow. The excerpt does not report dose precision, dose variability, or hopper-fill measurements as independently validated outcomes, nor does it describe a study that simultaneously inverted DEM parameters from feed-response data and independently validated those parameters using shear-cell testing. The surrounding discussion does link shear-cell-derived flow function/cohesion measurements to powder flow generally, and reports that colloidal silica can alter cohesion and FFC, but it does not connect those measurements directly to screw-dose precision in the cited material.
contexts.question: Which studies of powder screw feeder and auger dosing link powder properties or shear-cell flow function to dose precision, variability, screw rate and hopper fill? Do any simultaneously invert DEM parameters using feed response and validate independently against shear testing?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Klinger et al. (2022) as a study combining multiscale shear/friction characterization with pilot-scale hopper and screw-feeder experiments for milled woody biomass. It reports that bulk internal friction and apparent cohesion vary with granular-shear stress state, particle size, and particle-size distribution. The corresponding pilot-scale tests found that hopper critical arching distance and mass discharge rate depend strongly on overall particle size, while auger-feeder behavior is even more sensitive to particle size: smaller particles produced more consistent and stable flow and consumed less power. These findings are relevant to linking powder or biomass properties with feeder flow stability, but the excerpt does not mention dose precision, dosing variability, screw rate, or hopper-fill level as measured response variables. It also contains no evidence of a discrete-element-method (DEM) calibration or parameter inversion using feed response, nor of independent validation against shear-cell measurements. The cited article therefore provides a property-to-flow-performance comparison rather than the requested demonstration of simultaneous DEM parameter inversion and independent shear-test validation. No other powder screw-feeder or auger-dosing studies are included in the supplied excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt identifies several studies and approaches linking powder properties and operating variables to screw-feeder performance. It states that cohesion, particle descriptors, compressibility, rheology, flow, permeability, and porosity can significantly affect feeding. It also cites Engish and Muzzio’s statistical characterization of loss-in-weight feeders, which used relative standard deviation and ANOVA to evaluate the effects of feeder tooling, powder, and screw speed on feeder performance. Other cited work used data-driven response-surface or kriging models, multivariate methods, and semi-empirical models involving hopper powder pressure and feed factor. Physics-based models relate feed rate to volumetric efficiency, screw fullness, bulk density, screw speed, and screw geometry. The featured hybrid model estimates hopper stress, converts it to effective powder density through an empirical relationship, incorporates screw geometry and vortex-related volumetric efficiency, and predicts dynamic mass flow. DEM is described as useful for predicting packing, mass flow, and mixing, but requiring substantial computation and calibration of particle properties. The excerpt does not mention shear-cell flow-function testing, dose precision specifically, or a study that simultaneously inverts DEM parameters from feed-response data and independently validates them against shear testing.

The most directly relevant cited works are Dai and Grace’s experimental investigation of biomass granular screw feeding (2011), their study of tapered and extended screw sections (2008), and Sievers et al.’s “Design of Simulations and Validation Tests for Compression Screw Feeder Performance” (2018). contexts.context: The excerpt describes the DEM calibration methodology but does not provide the exact calibration data requested. Bhalode uses a bulk-property calibration strategy based on a drawdown test rather than reporting calibration from feeder discharge alone. The drawdown test measures four observables: mass in the lower container, angle of repose, shear angle, and maximum flowrate. These are intended to calibrate material parameters and address solution multiplicity. The excerpt explains that direct measurements such as static and rolling friction, shear modulus, and Young’s modulus are possible but require specialized equipment; bulk measurements are preferred because they are easier, cheaper, and computationally efficient. The DEM uses a Hertz–Mindlin contact model, with particle forces determined from overlap and material properties. For the feeder simulation, spherical cohesionless particles with standard rolling friction are used, with 1 mm radius and density of 1500 kg/m³; the feeder is run at fixed impellor and screw speeds. However, these pages do not state optimized cohesion or friction values, provide numerical comparisons between feeder mass flow and shear-cell or angle-of-repose data, or describe validation results. They also do not establish whether DEM parameters were inverted from feeder discharge itself or whether shear-cell results were independently tested. Those details would need to be checked in section 3.1 and subsequent calibration/validation results.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an inverse calibration procedure based on bulk measurements from a drawdown test, rather than clearly inverting DEM parameters from feeder discharge alone. Four DEM parameters were estimated from four measurements: angle of repose (30°), mass in the lower container (0.22 kg), shear angle (25°), and maximum flowrate (0.17 kg/s). The estimated parameters were particle static friction (PP_SF) = 0.4931, particle rolling friction (PP_RF) = 0.0383, particle coefficient of restitution (PP_COR) = 0.1851, and particle-wall static friction (PW_SF) = 0.195. The equations were solved by minimizing the sum of squared errors with GAMS/BARON, with an objective value of 4.2E-14. The dissertation also states that bulk measurements from the drawdown test depend on six DEM parameters, while four were estimated and other parameters were taken from the literature. Separately, feeder response-surface models identify PP_SF and PW_SF as important across all feed-factor parameters; PP_RF affects the maximum feed factor and restitution affects the decay parameter. The supplied pages mention feeder verification studies, but do not provide their results. They also do not demonstrate an independent shear-cell validation: “shear angle” is used as one drawdown-test calibration measurement, not clearly as a separately measured shear-cell result.

It states that the chapter’s associated publication is titled “Discrete element modeling for continuous powder feeding operation: Calibration and system analysis.” The stated motivation is that predictive models should incorporate detailed process understanding and powder material properties, because pharmaceutical powders can exhibit erratic flow behavior such as rat-holing and sticking to equipment walls. Feeder output is expressed as screw speed multiplied by a feed factor, with the feed factor related to powder compressibility and relative bulk density under screw compression. A Heckel-based feed-factor model is presented, with parameters representing maximum and minimum relative bulk density and the rate of change with feeder weight. The drawdown experiment provides four stated bulk measurements: angle of repose, shear angle, mass in the lower container, and maximum flowrate. Response-surface models correlate these measurements with DEM parameters, and the resulting system of equations is used to identify parameters for a new powder. Thus, the excerpt does not say that friction is directly measured; rather, friction-related DEM parameters are inferred through correlations with the drawdown bulk responses. Cohesion does not appear to be included in the presented feeder model as a developed feature: the conclusion lists contact models accounting for powder cohesion as something that “can also be added,” suggesting future or potential extension. The provided pages do not report whether feeder speed was varied; the verification study varies DEM material parameters, not explicitly feeder speed. They also do not mention an independent ring-shear characterization or validation. Therefore, the excerpt supports the drawdown measurements and calibration approach, but cannot establish feeder-speed variation or independent ring-shear checking.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general background on how cohesion affects continuous direct compression powder feeding, but it does not identify or discuss the Bhalode 2022 DEM powder-feeder chapter. It states that cohesion can restrict powder entry into converting screws, increase resistance within the swept screw volume, and promote electrostatic deposition and subsequent feeder dosing spikes. For characterization, it describes the Flow Function Coefficient (FFC) as a bulk flowability measure obtained from a ring shear tester. A normal consolidation force is applied to the powder bed, and the tangential force required to produce incipient failure is measured; a yield locus of shear stress versus normal stress is then used with Mohr–Coulomb theory to obtain principal yield stresses. The excerpt does not describe drawdown-based friction measurements, specify which measured quantities yield a friction coefficient, state whether feeder speed was varied, or indicate whether ring-shear results were independently checked. It therefore offers relevant general information about cohesion, feeding, and ring-shear characterization, but insufficient evidence to establish the procedures or validation used in the Bhalode chapter.

The most relevant original DEM/spreading studies cited are Parteli and Pöschel (2016), Lee et al. (2018), Marchais et al. (2021), Wu et al. (2022), Shaheen et al. (2021), Wang et al. contexts.context: This excerpt describes a numerical DEM study of powder spreading rather than an empirical validation against measured feeder or LPBF powder properties. MercuryDPM is used to simulate a blade spreading Ti-6Al-4V powder layer, with a 10 mm by 1 mm domain, a 100 µm tool gap, and a log-normal particle-size distribution (D10 = 24 µm, D50 = 37 µm, D90 = 56 µm). Cohesion is varied through the surface energy γ from 0 to 0.5 mJ/m², corresponding to Bond numbers from 0 to 272.3, using JKR adhesion and non-bonded van der Waals attraction. The stated aim is to assess powder quality through structural and surface measures, including spatial fluctuations of the free-surface height; the excerpt also notes that ordinary height distributions cannot capture spatial rearrangement or local heterogeneity. The model includes particle friction and viscoelastic Hertz–Mindlin contacts, but this passage does not discuss non-spherical particle shape, feeder calibration, experimental measurements, spreading packing-density validation, surface-coverage validation, or roughness comparisons with experiments. Consequently, it provides parameters and methodology for studying cohesion and PSD effects, but does not identify which original DEM papers empirically validated transfer from feeder-calibrated simulations to LPBF conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several original DEM studies relevant to powder spreading and empirical powder-bed properties. Nan et al. investigated spreader spacing and velocity in relation to powder shear bands and flow rate, reporting that mass flow rate increased linearly with spreader gap and was linearly dependent on velocity for a period before plateauing. Haeri et al. modeled rod-shaped particles and found that higher translational spreader velocities and larger particle aspect ratios increased surface roughness and packing density. Mussatto et al. studied spreader velocity and layer thickness and reported that reducing velocity improved powder-bed homogeneity. A further study by Haeri compared spreader geometries and found that a super-elliptical blade produced better powder-bed quality. The article also states that particle-size distribution affects powder flow and packing density, while local packing-density variation can cause porosity and unmelt defects. However, this excerpt does not provide direct evidence about cohesion or explicit feeder-calibrated DEM transferability to LPBF, nor does it clearly establish empirical validation against measured spreading coverage or roughness for each cited study. It does emphasize that particle morphology is difficult to control experimentally and that environmental conditions complicate comparisons, issues relevant to transferring DEM parameters from feeder calibration to LPBF conditions.
contexts.question: What original DEM powder spreading papers empirically validate spreading packing density, surface coverage or roughness against measured powder properties, and how do cohesion, particle shape and PSD affect ability to transfer feeder-calibrated DEM to LPBF?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify or bibliographically detail original DEM powder-spreading papers that empirically validate spreading packing density, surface coverage, or roughness against measured powder properties. It only states that DEM investigations have demonstrated effects of particle-size distribution (PSD) on packing density and surface coverage. Broad PSDs can improve packing because fines occupy voids between larger particles, but excessively broad distributions increase segregation and local variations in density and absorptivity. If layer thickness approaches the maximum particle size, particle filtering and jamming can reduce layer homogeneity. Particle shape is also important: spherical particles reduce friction, improve flowability and rearrangement, and promote homogeneous deposition, whereas irregular particles increase friction and hinder mobility, causing density fluctuations and poor coverage. Surface roughness similarly increases frictional resistance and reduces flowability, especially for fine powders. The excerpt does not directly discuss feeder-calibrated DEM transfer to LPBF, nor provide empirical comparisons between feeder measurements and LPBF spreading. It does, however, emphasize that process parameters and feedstock properties interact, implying that calibration transfer cannot rely on independent parameter adjustments and must account for PSD, morphology, cohesion-related flow behavior, layer thickness, recoater speed, and environmental conditions.
contexts.question: What original DEM powder spreading papers empirically validate spreading packing density, surface coverage or roughness against measured powder properties, and how do cohesion, particle shape and PSD affect ability to transfer feeder-calibrated DEM to LPBF?

The DEM model spread IN718 powder at 0.1 m/s and analyzed multilayer deposition, layerwise particle-size distributions, bed height, and packing density. In contrast, manual experiments sampled powder at three locations approximately 150 mm apart and found identical measured size distributions. It does, however, describe the material factors relevant to transferring a feeder-calibrated DEM model to LPBF. Cohesion is especially important for LPBF powders below 100 μm: van der Waals, electrostatic, capillary, and chemical interactions promote agglomeration and reduce mobility. DEM models that omit cohesion overestimate powder mobility and fail to reproduce observed powder-bed characteristics, while cohesive energy density is often a highly influential calibration parameter. Particle morphology and surface texture also affect friction, contact stiffness, rearrangement, compaction, and flowability; spherical particles generally improve rearrangement and packing, whereas rough surfaces increase resistance to motion. PSD affects both packing and cohesion: broad distributions can improve packing through interstitial filling, but larger fractions of fine particles increase cohesive effects and may worsen flowability. The excerpt cautions that conventional feeder or flowability metrics are only indicators because LPBF spreading occurs in constrained geometries with layer thicknesses comparable to particle diameters. Therefore, transferring DEM calibration from feeder tests to LPBF requires process-specific validation and attention to cohesion, shape, PSD, and surface characteristics.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents several limitations of dynamic powder-flow methods, but it does not specifically discuss Hall or Carney flow tests, humidity effects, static electricity, or the validation of spreadability metrics for LPBF. For cohesive powders, dynamic tests are difficult to interpret because adhesive contacts produce clumps and adhesion is coupled with particle friction. Rotating-drum measurements can also promote segregation, reducing powder homogeneity and affecting the measured rheological response; cohesive beds additionally have irregular free surfaces, making flow parameters difficult to determine. Impeller-based instruments may introduce artifacts such as slip at the impeller tip or walls and local aeration or jamming in the clearance. Dynamic ball indentation provides flow resistance as dynamic hardness, but hardness is not directly equivalent to unconfined yield strength. Relating the two requires a constraint factor, whose dependence on strain rate must be established. The impact-based test also does not directly control penetration depth, so iterative adjustment of test conditions may be needed, while crater volume and impact velocity must be measured. In powder spreading, the excerpt identifies empty patches, size segregation, and transient jamming—particularly with narrow spreader gaps—as observable defects or process indicators.
contexts.question: Which limitations of standard powder flow tests (Hall/Carney flow of cohesive fine powder, shear cells low vs high stress, humidity static electricity) and use of spreadability metrics for LPBF are documented?

contexts.context: The excerpt documents limitations of several dynamic powder-flow instruments, but it does not specifically discuss Hall or Carney flow tests, shear-cell testing at low versus high stresses, humidity effects, static electricity, or spreadability metrics for LPBF. For the Couette device, wall slip at the rotating inner cylinder can compromise measurements, the powder must be gripped at the walls to impose a no-slip condition, and the instrument requires a relatively large powder quantity. Its tall bed also experiences nonuniform gravity-induced stresses, anisotropic fabric, complex stress variations, and flow fields that may differ from the intended Couette shear. For the Anton Paar powder cell, results can vary with impeller geometry, and measurements taken at a fixed position may not represent the whole bed because of segregation, local aeration, and slipping. For the FT4 rheometer, Basic Flow Energy and Specific Energy are empirical dynamic measures based on impeller penetration and withdrawal. The article notes ongoing uncertainty about whether these energies reflect bulk friction or shear viscosity, and reports that a consistent direct correlation between measured flow energy and bulk mechanical or rheological properties has not been established. The excerpt only briefly connects powder flowability with additive manufacturing and provides no documented LPBF spreadability metric limitations.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents several broad limitations of conventional cohesive-powder flow testing. Powder-flow prediction is highly sensitive to material properties, particle form, humidity, and tribo-electric charging, so environmental variability—including static-electric effects—complicates reproducible measurements. Quasi-static bulk-failure testing is described as well established, but the resulting bulk parameters depend on applied load and consolidation history and are sensitive to shear strain rate. Consequently, standard shear-cell methods do not adequately represent dynamic or high-rate flow: the authors state that no shear cell is available for characterising bulk parameters in the dynamic regime, while only a small number of powder rheometers quantify resistance to motion as a function of shear rate. Different commercial testers can also produce different quantitative values because cohesive powders form clusters whose size and packing depend on stress history and bulk structure. The excerpt emphasizes that low-stress testing is desirable in some applications, particularly where only small quantities of powder are available. For additive manufacturing, powder spreading is identified as critical, making flow and spreadability important concerns for processes such as LPBF. However, these pages do not specifically document Hall or Carney flow-test limitations, nor do they define or evaluate particular spreadability metrics for LPBF; those details would require later sections or another source.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes Faqih et al. (2006) as an experimental/computational study of unconfined cohesive powder flow using a gravity-driven rotating-cylinder device (GDR) coupled to downstream hoppers with outlet angles of 35°, 45°, 55°, 65°, and 75°. Powder discharge and avalanching are monitored through a load cell, whose analog signal is sampled at 2000 Hz for 100 s. The measured weight is divided by material density to obtain directly comparable volume-related data. The analysis applies a Fast Fourier transform and identifies the approximately 1–5 Hz frequency range as the meaningful region associated with avalanching; empty-cylinder and free-flowing glass-bead controls show little organized signal in this range. After filtering and transforming back to the time domain, the variance of the signal quantifies changes in the material center of mass and is used to compare powders across rotation rates, fill levels, and powder types. The excerpt explicitly states that signal variance is proportional to cohesion and that larger variance generally indicates stronger cohesion and larger avalanches. contexts.context: Faqih et al. (2006) directly couples an experimental gravity-discharge/flow signal with a discrete-element-method (DEM) model for unconfined cohesive powder flow. The computational objective is explicitly to relate inter-particle cohesive strength to GDR measurements. Cohesion is represented through a square-well potential producing a constant-intensity normal force during contact, parameterized by the Bond number K = Fcohes/mg. In the reported simulations, K was varied from 0 to 90: no avalanches occurred below K = 30, while discrete avalanches appeared for moderate and higher cohesion, particularly K > 45; values above 90 generated avalanches comparable to system size. Experimental flow behavior was quantified from the variance or standard deviation of the center-of-mass/weight signal versus vessel rotation rate. Increasing cohesion generally increased avalanche magnitude and the relative standard deviation, although overlapping avalanches at high speeds reduced the measured standard deviation. DEM validation used visual flow-region shape and local angle of repose, avalanche size, and material dilation. The excerpt does not provide details of a standard shear-cell validation protocol, nor does it discuss screw feeders. Therefore, it supports comparison with a screw feeder only at the general level: both systems can be studied through cohesion-dependent flow behavior, but the cited work concerns rotating-vessel gravity flow and avalanche/GDR metrics rather than continuous screw conveyance, torque, throughput, or feeder discharge.

Six particle–particle input parameters were studied: Young’s modulus, particle size, coefficient of restitution, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density. contexts.context: The excerpt supports using FT4 dynamic yield strength (DYS) and shear-cell tests in a staged, complementary way rather than attempting to identify all DEM parameters from one test. FT4 DYS is strongly affected by contact cohesion, represented here by surface energy, and is also responsive to rolling and sliding friction. Rolling friction produces a particularly strong DYS response, rising sharply up to approximately CoRF = 0.30, while sliding friction has a non-monotonic response with a peak near CoSF = 0.1. Because DYS is “extremely sensitive” to surface energy, the stated recommended procedure is to fix the friction parameters first and then calibrate surface energy against DYS. The shear cell provides a distinct response for checking frictional behavior: changing CoSF from 0.40 to 1.0 had little effect, CoSF = 0.1 increased critical-state shear, and increasing CoRF from 0.01 to 1.0 raised the critical shear value from 1008 to 1183 Pa. Although shear cell response is also affected by surface energy, it is less sensitive than DYS, making it suitable as an independent validation test after calibration. The excerpt does not establish complete parameter uniqueness; separate resolution requires one-at-a-time or multi-parameter studies and validation against both tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using FT4 dynamic measurements and shear-cell measurements as complementary tests, but it does not demonstrate that interparticle friction, rolling resistance, and contact cohesion can each be identified independently. FT4 BFE and SE respond to frictional contacts, particle shape, particle size, cohesion, moisture, and strain rate. In particular, dynamic tests are described as more sensitive to frictional contact forces, while SE has been correlated with the cohesion parameter measured in the FT4 rotational shear cell. DEM studies cited in the excerpt identify particle friction, rotational resistance, cohesion, and capillary forces as contributors to measured flow energy, but the reported measurements are coupled responses rather than unique parameter measurements. Therefore, a shear cell could reasonably be used to calibrate or constrain DEM parameters—especially bulk shear strength/cohesion and friction-related behavior—while FT4 dynamic yield or flow-energy data could provide complementary calibration targets sensitive to dynamic frictional and cohesive effects. However, treating FT4 as independent validation after calibrating the DEM with the same shear-cell-derived properties requires caution: FT4 should be considered independent only if its operating conditions, observables, and data were not used in parameter fitting. contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant background for evaluating a cohesive-powder micro-feeder study, but it does not discuss Peter Chung-Hsien Hou’s 2024 work or report its specific experimental variables and validation methods. It describes a DEM investigation of feeding performance in which adhesive stiffness (Kadh) and conveying-impeller rotation rate were varied. At a fixed rotation rate, increasing cohesion affected particle translational velocity, while across the tested conditions, conveying speed had a greater influence on hopper particle velocity than cohesion. Increasing Kadh reduced average mass discharged per watt and, above a threshold, produced arching or bridging. These structures caused inconsistent screw filling and irregular mass flow. The review recommends mapping transient cohesive behavior while varying particle properties, feeder geometry, and rotational speed, and suggests using a more commercially representative feeder with a hopper agitator and twin-screw conveying elements. contexts.context: The excerpt reports empirical optimization of double-screw powder feeding, not inverse DEM characterization. For cohesive CCS, 15/7 non-compression gave low standard deviation, good repeatability/stability, and was recommended; 7/7 compression showed poor SD above 0.4 g/h. For non-flowing APAP, 25/25 compression was recommended: it produced the highest flow (about 1.9–3.3 g/h above 25/25 non-compression), low SD, and favorable stability. Tests used a 30° screw angle and inner pitches of 7, 10, and 15 mm; increasing pitch only slightly increased flow, while 7 mm gave the most consistent stability.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes conventional powder characterization, not auger-based inverse inference. Particle size/shape was measured by QIC/PIC after dispersing 2 g at 100 m/s, in triplicate. True, bulk, and tapped densities were measured in triplicate, with \(\rho_p=W_p/V_p\), \(\rho_b=W/V_b\), and \(\rho_t=W/V_t\), following USP<616>. Flowability used Hausner ratio/Carr Index and Brookfield shear testing. The flow function coefficient was \(ffc=\sigma_1/\sigma_c\), derived from yield loci using at least three normal loads; testing also assessed cohesion, internal/wall friction, and compressibility.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt studies a pneumatic piston micro-feeder, not an auger or DEM-based inverse characterization. Mean feed rate follows \(\dot m_{p,b}=S\rho_bA_b/(1-C)\), with \(A_b=71.18\text{ mm}^2\), and increases linearly with piston speed. Airflow and pressure strongly affect stability: MCC used 25 kPa, while more cohesive APAP used 30–50 kPa and roughly twice MCC’s air mass flow. APAP (Hausner ratio >1.60) required 7 versus 4 mm/min piston speed, had a 6.9-minute acceleration phase, and showed adhesion/accumulation. The authors explicitly say slope relationships to cohesion, particle size, and density remain unconfirmed.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides background for comparing Hall/Carney funnel methods with FT4-type powder-rheology testing, but it does not report the specific Marchetti and Hulme-Smith (2021) experiments or numerical comparison outcomes, and it does not mention ASTM D7891 by name. It characterizes Hall flow as closer to additive-manufacturing conditions than some alternatives, while noting that it is unsuitable for cohesive powders and may be most useful for ranking powder qualities, particularly for EBM powders. The Carney funnel is discussed in relation to Hausner ratio: tap and apparent density were not connected to Carney-funnel behavior, whereas Hausner-ratio values were related to flow rates in some studies. The review emphasizes that flowability is equipment- and test-dependent, so results from different methods should not automatically be treated as equivalent. FT4-related shear testing is presented as potentially more relevant to spreadability or powder-layer formation: ultimate yield strength, cohesion, and flow function measured using a powder rheometer correlated well with observed layer-formation quality. Thus, the excerpt supports evaluating test relevance through correlation with actual layer formation, while warning that Hall/Carney outcomes may be limited or method-specific.

It does report broader correlations among powder-flow tests and metrics that are relevant to interpreting such a comparison. Major principal stress (MPS) was more strongly correlated with Hausner ratio, specific energy, and angle of repose, while cohesion and ultimate yield strength correlated more strongly with compressibility and angle of repose. contexts.context: The excerpt reports Hall- and Carney-funnel flow-rate tests, including the particle-size-to-outlet ratio D50(Doutlet)−1 and outcomes such as jamming, ratholing, and measured flow time. For powders of similar chemistry and production method, finer fractions showed greater tendency to jam; samples 1, 3, 4, 7, and 11 jammed in at least one funnel, sample 2 formed a rathole, and sample 5—the coarsest powder—flowed through both funnels. The discussion attributes these observations to cohesive behavior and, for coarser particles, possible interlocking mechanisms. The study also examined angle of repose, specific energy, compressibility, Hausner ratio, flow function, yield-stress-related metrics, conditioned bulk density, and shear-cell parameters. Although several indicators were mutually correlated, only 15 of 59 statistically significant relationships were judged representative using adjusted R² > 0.7. The provided pages do not mention an FT4 test, ASTM D7891, a direct Hall/Carney-versus-FT4 comparison, or spreadability testing/outcomes. Therefore, these pages support conclusions about Hall/Carney funnel behavior and its relation to powder size and flowability indicators, but do not establish FT4 ASTM D7891 or spreadability relevance.

The FT4-related measurements reported here are represented by metrics such as basic flowability energy (BFE), specific energy (SE), compressibility (CPS), conditioned bulk density (CBD), and shear-cell measures including major principal stress (MPS), cohesion, and ultimate yield strength. BFE showed weak correlation with most other metrics, which the authors attribute to confinement and compression during testing. By contrast, SE, Hausner ratio, compressibility, and angle of repose were inter-correlated; CBD correlated strongly with most metrics, and representative relationships were reported for CBD–HR and MPS9–CBD. The excerpt does not explicitly identify ASTM D7891 or provide a direct FT4-versus-ASTM comparison, so no exact ASTM D7891 outcome can be substantiated from this passage. Spreadability is application-relevant but remains future work: the authors state that a procedure for characterising steel-powder spreadability had yet to be established. They also caution that a test should replicate the powder’s specific application conditions, although this may not always be possible for additive-manufacturing spreading.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a qualitative, rather than numerical, dependence on pre-shear conditions. The FT4 powder rheometer produced lower yield and steady-state stress values than the other shear devices because its pre-shearing protocol differed; therefore, FT4 stresses should not be directly equated with values from the Schulze ring shear tester without accounting for the preparation history and protocol. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative relation between pre-shear stress and the measured response, nor does it specify an equivalent pre-shear stress for the two instruments. Across eight chemically identical limestone powders, bulk cohesion decreased as particle size increased up to approximately 150 μm, consistent with weaker interparticle cohesion for larger particles. Above 150 μm, cohesion increased slightly, while bulk friction increased considerably, plausibly because of particle interlocking. Removing fines from coarse powders reduced both cohesion and bulk density but had negligible influence on bulk friction. Thus, cohesion cannot be interpreted as a simple monotonic function of size over the full range, and results from different tests cannot be treated as identical merely because the same powder is tested: device-specific shear and pre-shear protocols affect yield and steady-flow stresses.

contexts.context: For the eight limestone powders, measurements covered normal stresses of 5, 20, and 35 kPa. Increasing normal stress raised bulk density and cohesive strength, with a stronger effect for finer powders; however, the excerpt does not provide a separate numerical law relating cohesion specifically to pre-shear stress. Particle-size dependence separates near a median size of 150 μm. Below this threshold, contact cohesion dominates, but its influence weakens as particle size increases: bulk cohesion decreases toward nearly zero, while bulk density increases monotonically. Above 150 μm, the behavior is non-monotonic and less straightforward: bulk cohesion initially slightly increases with particle size and then decreases, while bulk friction angles increase. Removing fines from coarse samples substantially reduces both bulk density and cohesion, showing that fines are the principal source of cohesion, whereas friction angles are little affected. FT4 and Schulze RST-01 yield loci cannot be quantitatively equated as though they were identical tests. RST-01 values are consistently slightly higher, whereas FT4 gives a significantly lower locus, attributed to different pre-shear protocols. Thus, although qualitative trends may agree, protocol-dependent differences can produce considerable deviations and must be interpreted cautiously.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a partial ASTM mapping for additive-manufacturing metal-powder characterization. ASTM B214 addresses sieve analysis and particle-size measurement; ASTM B822 covers particle-size distribution by light scattering; ASTM B213 specifies Hall flowmeter-funnel flow-rate testing; ASTM B964 specifies Carney-funnel flow-rate testing; and ASTM B527 covers tap density. The report concludes that standards for sampling, particle size, flow, and density are already available and appear readily applicable to additive-manufacturing powders. It also identifies important limitations: morphology, chemical composition, and thermal-property measurements are covered by relatively few standards, and their standardization may be more difficult. The excerpt does not provide information on ASTM B212, D7891, or D6773, nor does it identify the Gibbons, Govender, and van der Merwe review or give a complete test-selection matrix. Therefore, it can substantiate the portions of a review concerning B213, B964, B214, B822, and B527, along with the general recommendation to combine established size, flow, density, and sampling tests with additional characterization of morphology, chemistry, and thermal behavior. Specific limitations, applicability conditions, and recommendations for the omitted standards require the cited review or other source material.

It does, however, identify important limitations and recommendations for powder characterization in powder-bed-fusion applications. Angle of repose (AoR) is described as a useful flowability and cohesion indicator; a low value, typically 35 degrees or less, suggests lower cohesion and better flowability. ISO 4324 is mentioned for powders and granules, but the review states that no standard method specifically exists for metal powders used in PBF. Rotating-drum avalanche testing is considered well suited to PBF because drum speed can be adjusted to approximate recoater speeds, although no publicly available standard exists for that method. Shear testing can use Jenike, Schulze, or Freeman instruments. Freeman rheometers are particularly useful for low-stress dynamic flow conditions resembling PBF and can measure BFE, flow rate, consolidation indices, conditioned bulk density, specific energy, and aerated energy. Conditioning is recommended to reduce stress history and improve repeatability. ASTM C177 is cited for guarded-hot-plate thermal measurements, but the excerpt notes that guidance is needed when applying it to metal powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM calibration strategy for Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V powders using a Revolution Powder Analyzer/revolving drum as the experimental reference. Calibration uses a surrogate model to vary DEM parameters simultaneously and account for parameter interdependencies, while matching the simulated bulk response to experimental observations. The excerpt does not identify the precise measured target variables or calibration metrics, but it characterizes the drum as providing steady granular flow, repeatable measurements, and robust flowability metrics. Computational cost is reduced through geometric down-scaling rather than coarse-graining, while retaining the real particle-size distribution and keeping system dimensions substantially larger than particle size. The scaling approach is validated by running the calibrated model at multiple scaling factors. The simulations also examine avalanche progression and size segregation in the drum. A key limitation is application transfer: although the drum calibration represents rotating-drum flow, the authors state that further work is needed to determine whether the calibrated parameter state reproduces the granular dynamical response relevant to powder-bed recoating. contexts.context: Sani et al. (2026) calibrate DEM models for two representative PBF-EB alloy powders, Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V (Ti64), using a rotating/revolution drum and surrogate-model analysis. The measured calibration targets are the break, rest, and avalanche energies, which characterize bulk flow responses. The approach uses geometrically down-scaled DEM simulations while retaining the real particle size distribution and matching dynamic behavior through Froude-number scaling. Scaling validation across tested drum sizes found a linear relationship between the bulk energy responses and drum radius, supporting the method within the investigated range. The calibration also identified particle–particle friction, rolling friction, and surface energy as dominant parameters, while particle–tool interactions had limited influence in this setup. Important limitations affect transfer to powder-bed recoating: matching the Froude number alone does not ensure similarity in all relevant dimensionless groups, especially for cohesive fine powders; the study does not establish a direct quantitative relationship between rotating-drum behavior and AM powder spreading; and segregation mechanisms differ between drum avalanching and recoating. In the drum, larger particles move toward the wall and surface while fines concentrate centrally through kinetic sieving, whereas recoating involves horizontal shear and fine-particle trapping along walls. Further validation with multiple drum diameters is planned.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM calibration framework for Ti64 and Inconel 718 powders in a rotating-drum context. The candidate calibration variables are particle–particle and particle–tool friction coefficient, rolling friction coefficient, and van der Waals surface energy. A DOE is used to generate DEM responses, followed by ANOVA to identify influential factors and interactions. Particle–tool parameters are found to have considerably less influence than particle–particle parameters and are therefore fixed at the midpoints of their ranges for subsequent calibration. A surrogate model is constructed from three multi-input, single-output polynomial response models, representing break energy (BE), rest energy (RE), and avalanche energy (AE). The calibration optimization seeks parameter values whose surrogate-predicted responses match experimental target mean values; AE is defined as the difference between BE and RE. Validation uses an error threshold based on the standard deviation of the experimental measurements. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the rotating-drum DEM scaling and calibration framework for Ti64 and Inconel 718 powders. The reduced simulation drum preserves dynamic similarity through Froude-number scaling: reducing the drum radius by five requires increasing angular velocity by √5. Thus, the experimental drum speed of 0.6 RPM (100-second period) is represented by 1.34 RPM (44.7-second period) in simulation. The Ti64 and Inconel 718 models contain approximately 110,000 and 71,000 particles, respectively, and use a 0.5 µs timestep confirmed to be below the Rayleigh limit and numerically converged. The DEM formulation includes Hertz–Mindlin–Deresiewicz contact forces, rolling resistance, and van der Waals adhesion, which is considered important for metallic powders with particle sizes of tens of microns. Simulations use the GPU-based Demify solver. The calibration strategy seeks to reduce computational cost by identifying active parameters that significantly affect bulk powder behavior and excluding weakly influential parameters. However, these pages do not specify the measured target variables, report validation results for the Froude-scaled surrogate, or discuss limitations when transferring rotating-drum calibration to powder-bed recoating. contexts.context: The excerpt describes powder-specific DEM surrogate calibration for Inconel 718 and Ti64 in a rotating drum. The measured target variables are break energy, rest energy, and avalanche energy. Calibration uses separate polynomial surrogate models, retaining statistically significant friction, rolling-friction, surface-energy, interaction, and quadratic terms; the active factors differ between the two powders. The objective function minimizes the root-sum-square discrepancy between experimental targets and surrogate predictions, with a 5% error threshold. Final calibrated inter-particle parameters are: Inconel 718—particle friction 0.76, rolling friction 0.08, and surface energy 0.16 mJ/m²; Ti64—0.78, 0.14, and 0.015 mJ/m², respectively. Simulated versus target errors are 0.22%, 0.25%, and 0.04% for Inconel 718 break, rest, and avalanche energies, and 0.25%, 0.42%, and 3.83% for Ti64. The drum is geometrically scaled by 1:5, with angular velocity adjusted to preserve the Froude number; normalized energy and time enable comparison. Three additional simulations using different drum radii were conducted to validate scaling. The excerpt does not discuss direct powder-bed recoating performance or limitations, so applicability to recoating remains unestablished here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the NIST Powder Spreading Testbed (PST), a compact apparatus intended to mimic commercial LPBF recoating while reducing powder consumption. It uses a controlled recoater carriage driven by a stepper motor and ball screw, with a vertical actuator for baseplate height and a viewing glass for side imaging. Two powder-heap preparation methods are provided: a stencil method, which creates a narrower and more convenient heap for single-layer spreading, and a cylinder-based method, which produces a more distributed heap and is better suited to multilayer experiments. The authors explicitly note that heap-creation method can affect spreading behavior, particularly the powder density in front of the recoater. The PST also supports controlled recoater speeds and gap/height adjustment, and its vibration behavior was characterized over 1–20 cm/s; most measured vibration amplitudes were below 1 µm RMS, although an additional motor-related spectral peak appeared near 18–19 cm/s. This material is potentially relevant as an independent recoating platform for studying process variables and validating spread-bed uniformity, but the excerpt does not report measurements of spread-bed density uniformity or blade force, nor does it discuss Brika and Brailovski or feeder-fingerprint independence.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates simulation-based inverse calibration for powder flow, but in a rotating powder-analyzer (RPA) drum rather than an auger feeder. DOE/ANOVA surrogate models related break, rest, and avalanche energies to sliding friction (X1), rolling friction (X2), and surface energy (X3), with powder-specific sensitivities. Calibrated values were Inconel 718: friction 0.76, rolling friction 0.08, surface energy 0.16 mJ/m²; Ti64: 0.78, 0.14, 0.015 mJ/m². Simulations matched targets within 5% (maximum Ti64 avalanche error 3.83%); 18–19 additional points refined calibration.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes conventional powder-flow characterization, not auger-based inference. Schulze RST-01 is widely used to obtain yield and wall-yield loci; the smaller RST-XS handles only “3.5 ml to 70 ml” versus 204 ml for RST-01. The FT4 Powder Rheometer offers automated testing with minimal operator intervention and follows ASTM D7891-15, including blade conditioning and controlled pre-shear/shear. Direct shear devices follow ASTM D6128; drawbacks include laborious filling, sample conditioning, operator influence, and possible powder ejection. No feeder discharge, DEM inversion, or validation linking feeder fingerprints to these tests is reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents a feeder-based DEM calibration approach. Stepwise/AIC/BIC regression and response-surface models relate feeder outputs \(FF_{max}\), \(FF_{min}\), and decay coefficient \(\beta\) to DEM parameters. Particle–particle and particle–wall static friction affect all outputs; rolling friction mainly affects initially full-hopper flow, while restitution affects powder transfer and \(\beta\). Shear modulus was insignificant. Four bulk drawdown measurements (angle of repose \(30^\circ\), lower-container mass 0.22 kg, shear angle \(25^\circ\), maximum flowrate 0.17 kg/s) were solved for four DEM parameters, yielding PP_SF 0.4931, PP_RF 0.0383, PP_COR 0.1851, and PW_SF 0.195.

contexts.context: Haeri (2017) uses device-scale DEM to optimize blade spreaders for powder-bed fusion, targeting minimum bed void fraction rather than characterizing feeder discharge. Simulations use rod-shaped grains to reduce computational cost, then realistic 3D grain shapes generated by a new multi-sphere approximation (MSA). Blade geometry is parameterized by three super-ellipse parameters; optimized profiles achieve bed volume fractions near critical values and performance comparable to, or better than, a counter-rotating roller. The excerpt emphasizes particle size distribution, morphology, angle of repose, flowability, and bulk behavior as important to spread quality, but reports no auger-based inverse property inference or validation against shear-cell tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports DEM simulations of powder spreaders, not inverse characterization. Blade-head geometry strongly affects packed-bed volume fraction: optimized convex profiles increased \(ϕ_s\) from about 0.4 to 0.58, while concave \(n_s=0.5\) profiles could clog near blades and degrade the bed. Linear profiles (\(n_s=1\)) performed better when shorter and wider. An optimum tested shape used \(n_s=5\), \(a_s=100D_{sph}\), \(b_s=10D_{sph}\); \(b_s=50D_{sph}\) was selected for realistic manufacture. Stair-step STL discretization produced volume errors up to 14.676%.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?

No. # Can an auger doser serve as a powder-characterization instrument?

**Short answer:** I found close precedents for each *part* of the proposed approach, but **no verified publication that combines all three steps**: infer cohesive and frictional DEM parameters *from the measured response of a small screw doser itself*; independently test those inferences against shear-cell flow properties; and use them to predict powder-bed spreadability. This is a qualified literature finding, not a claim that no such study exists. Two especially pertinent El-Kassem auger-dosing publications were identifiable but their full texts were unavailable for verification. (jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 71-77, hou2024developmentofa pages 200-207)

## Closest precedents—and the missing step

- **Screw feeding modeled by DEM:** López and colleagues simulated how changing particle adhesion and screw speed affects paracetamol feeding. Greater adhesion reduced mass discharged per unit power; sufficiently strong adhesion caused bridging, incomplete screw-pitch filling, and irregular flow. This demonstrates that feeder output contains information about cohesion, **not** that cohesion was recovered by inverting an experimental dosing fingerprint or checked against an independent shear test. The accessible account describes adhesive *stiffness*, which should not be relabeled as the SJKR cohesion-energy-density parameter. (jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6)
- **Inversion followed by feeder simulation:** Bhalode inferred particle sliding friction, rolling friction, restitution, and wall friction from a **separate drawdown experiment** measuring repose angle, shear angle, collected mass, and maximum discharge rate. The resulting DEM analysis related those parameters to a screw feeder’s feed-factor-versus-hopper-weight curve. Crucially, the feeder model used **cohesionless** spheres at fixed screw and impeller speeds; its calibration data were not the feeder response, and independent ring-shear validation was not demonstrated. (bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 45-49, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 71-77, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 67-71)
- **Inclined microfeeder plus conventional characterization:** Hou tested a screw microfeeder at an inclination of **30°**, varying screw/agitator settings and measuring flow-rate variation, repeatability, and stability. The powders were also characterized with a shear-cell-based flow-function measurement. This is particularly close experimentally, but the accessible thesis describes equipment optimization rather than DEM inversion of its feeding signals or DEM-to-shear-cell validation. (hou2024developmentofa pages 200-207, hou2024developmentofa pages 1-5, hou2024developmentofa pages 106-108)
- **Other complementary examples:** El-Kassem and colleagues used designed DEM simulations, including SJKR cohesion, to study how contact parameters affect *funnel* discharge, repose angle, and packing and compared calibrated bulk responses with experiments—not a screw-derived inverse characterization. Klinger and colleagues measured shear properties alongside pilot-scale screw-feeder performance in milled biomass, without demonstrating feeder-based DEM inversion. Faqih and colleagues related cohesion-dependent, intermittent *rotating-vessel* flow signals to DEM and hopper behavior, rather than screw dosing or independent shear-cell validation. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, klinger2022multiscaleshearproperties pages 1-2, faqih2006anexperimentalcomputationalapproach pages 8-9, faqih2006anexperimentalcomputationalapproach pages 1-2)

**Positioning:** The defensible novelty is *feeder-as-sensor inverse calibration, using a multistate dosing fingerprint, followed by genuinely held-out bulk-flow and recoating tests*. It is **not** the first DEM screw-feeder study, the first inverse DEM calibration, or the first comparison between feeder performance and conventional powder properties. (jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 71-77, hou2024developmentofa pages 200-207, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 8-10)

## A discriminating validation study

1. **Fit only dosing observations.** At controlled reservoir fill, preparation history, print material/surface state, and humidity, obtain replicate mass-per-revolution curves over tilt and speed, no-flow probabilities, tap-released masses, and stop–afterflow traces. Model the balance’s response delay separately from physical afterflow. Fit joint distributions or a likelihood for both continuous mass and intermittent events; mean throughput alone can conceal bridging. Varying fill matters: feeder DEM work finds different contact parameters important at high and low hopper weights. (jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6, faqih2006anexperimentalcomputationalapproach pages 8-9, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 67-71)
2. **Infer an *effective contact-model parameter set*, not intrinsic material constants by fiat.** Treat particle-size distribution and density as measured inputs; estimate particle–particle sliding/rolling friction, particle–PLA/PETG friction or adhesion, and SJKR cohesion with uncertainty. Test parameter identifiability by examining correlations and alternative sets that reproduce the same fingerprint. Drawdown DEM work explicitly illustrates that multiple contact-parameter combinations can give the same bulk response. In SJKR, cohesion energy density enters a **contact-force law**; a shear-cell’s macroscopic cohesion is a **yield-locus quantity**, so numerical equality is neither required nor expected. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 41-45, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 67-71)
3. **Make validation independent.** Hold FT4 shear-cell measurements under ASTM D7891 and Schulze ring-shear measurements under ASTM D6773 out of the fit. Predict their yield loci, bulk cohesion, internal-friction behavior, and flow-function coefficients at *specified consolidation stresses* using the feeder-inferred DEM ensemble. Compare intervals and trends, not just a single powder ranking. FT4 and ring-shear values can differ because conditioning and preshear protocols differ; an eight-powder inter-device study found lower FT4 yield/steady stresses under its protocol. Measure wall friction against the actual printed polymer separately where possible. If shear measurements are used to tune a parameter, report them as **calibration**, not independent validation. (wang2016usingmultivariateanalysis pages 43-47, hou2024developmentofa pages 106-108, shi2018effectofparticle pages 17-18, shi2018effectofparticle pages 5-7)
4. **Use the other standard tests as complementary checks, with their proper scope.** B213/B964 measure Hall/Carney funnel flow; B212/B527 measure apparent/tap density; B214/B822 address sieve/light-scattering particle sizes. Record non-flow through a funnel as an outcome rather than forcing a flow-time number: in a study of cohesive steel powders, jamming made both Hall and Carney flow rates unsuitable for discriminating samples. Density, size distribution, repose angle, and controlled loss-on-drying/humidity experiments help diagnose packing, fines, and moisture effects, but none independently measures a unique DEM cohesion coefficient. (cooke2012propertiesofmetal pages 23-27, cooke2012propertiesofmetal pages 27-28, marchetti2021flowabilityofsteel pages 9-10, ghadiri2020cohesivepowderflow pages 1-2)
5. **Test spreadability directly.** On the alloy powders, use a controlled blade or roller recoating experiment, with specified layer gap, speed, substrate, and atmosphere; hold measured deposited-layer density, spatial coverage/empty patches, and surface roughness out of the feeder fit. Experimental recoating and DEM studies show why this is necessary: cohesion can reduce layer packing and increase roughness, while gap and spreading conditions introduce jamming and defects that feeder throughput does not represent. A recent surrogate-based DEM calibration to *rotating-drum* responses for Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V likewise explicitly leaves transfer to recoating unestablished. (habiba2023powderspreadingmechanism pages 2-4, roy2024structuralfluctuationsin pages 16-18, ghadiri2020cohesivepowderflow pages 5-6, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 12-13, whiting2023powderspreadingtestbed pages 9-12)

**Feasibility caveat:** At the stated **26–30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution**, a full-grid Bayesian inversion would be costly. An initial sensitivity/design-of-experiments screen, a surrogate with simulation-error checks, and sequential simulations focused on parameter combinations that the observed fingerprint can distinguish are better justified than attempting to fit every contact parameter simultaneously. Published DEM calibrations already use response surfaces or surrogates, but success within the calibration device does **not** establish transfer to a shear cell or recoater. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, bhalode2022multiscalemodelingand pages 41-45, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 1-2, sani2026efficientdemcalibration pages 8-10)

**Limit of this assessment:** The bibliographic search identified El-Kassem and colleagues’ *Experimental study and discrete element simulation of auger dosing of different pharmaceutical powders* (2018, DOI **10.1002/pamm.201800261**) and *A multivariate statistical approach to analyze the impact of material attributes and process parameters on the quality performance of an auger dosing process* (2020, DOI **10.1016/j.jddst.2020.101950**), but their full texts could not be inspected here. Their existence precludes an absolute first-in-literature claim; the available evidence does not establish that either performed the complete feeder-response inversion **and independent shear-cell validation** posed in the question. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, jonessalkey2023reviewingtheimpact pages 4-6, bascone2020hybridmechanisticempiricalapproach pages 4-8)

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Has anyone used the dosing or discharge response of a small screw or auger feeder or powder doser (mass per revolution as a function of tilt angle and screw speed, flow intermittency, afterflow) together with discrete element simulations to inversely infer powder properties such as cohesion or interparticle friction, that is, used the feeder itself as a powder characterization instrument, and validated the inferred values against shear-cell or other standard flowability measurements?
